recipe.history:
Shrimp and prawns — the two terms are often used interchangeably in American usage, though biologically they belong to different suborders — have been central to human diets for millennia across every coastal civilization in the world. In the Gulf of Mexico and the American South, shrimping has been a foundational industry and culinary tradition since before European colonization, with indigenous peoples of the Gulf Coast harvesting wild shrimp in vast quantities using nets and weirs. The brown, white, and pink shrimp species native to Gulf waters became the backbone of Louisiana and Gulf Coast Creole cuisine, appearing in gumbo, étouffée, barbecue shrimp, and po'boys. Gulf prawns — larger, meatier, and sweeter than their Atlantic counterparts — are the species most associated with Southern cooking, and their harvest shaped the culture, economy, and diet of coastal communities from Texas to Florida. In Southeast Asia, where the term prawn more precisely applies to true freshwater prawns of the Macrobrachium genus, shrimp and prawn pastes, dried shrimp, and fresh prawns have been pillars of cooking traditions for at least two thousand years, with shrimp paste — bagoong, belacan, kapi — appearing in the foundational sauces of Thai, Vietnamese, Malaysian, and Filipino cuisine.

In Los Angeles, the confluence of Gulf Coast shrimping culture, Southeast Asian immigration, and California's obsession with fresh, high-quality seafood created a unique culinary identity around prawns and shrimp in the second half of the twentieth century. The Cajun and Creole restaurants of South Los Angeles — brought by the Great Migration of Black Southerners who transplanted Gulf Coast food culture to California — served shrimp dishes that had no equivalent in traditional California cooking. Meanwhile, the enormous Vietnamese and Thai communities of the San Gabriel Valley created a parallel world of shrimp-forward cooking centered on nuoc cham, tamarind, and lemongrass. The LA shrimp aioli burger emerged from this collision: Gulf-seared prawns as a topping on a beef patty, with a shrimp-infused mayonnaise that carried the sweet, briny intensity of the crustacean through every layer of the bite. It is a Los Angeles burger — confident, hybrid, and more than the sum of its influences.

The first time I ate a prawn on a burger I was at a small counter restaurant in the Silverlake neighborhood of Los Angeles, and the owner had placed two whole seared prawns, shell-on, on top of a beef patty with nothing but a pool of garlic aioli under them. I did not know what to do — I had never eaten a burger with something that looked back at me — and so I just bit into the whole thing, shell and all, and the crunch of the caramelized shell against the soft bun and the juicy patty was a revelation. I drove back to that restaurant three times in two weeks trying to memorize the flavor. The shrimp aioli in this recipe is my attempt to reconstruct what that garlic-aioli base was doing, and the seared gulf prawns are my tribute to those shell-on beauties that changed my understanding of what a burger could include.

A prawn-topped burger is an argument about richness, and medium rare is the only way to manage it correctly. Gulf prawns bring sweetness, brine, and a firm, yielding texture; the shrimp aioli brings fat and concentrated crustacean flavor; the bun brings softness and starch. In this context, the beef patty is the anchor — it must be assertive enough to anchor all that richness rather than disappearing beneath it. A medium-rare patty at 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit has the rendered-fat moisture and the yielding pink center that can stand alongside prawns without being overwhelmed or without overwhelming them. A well-done patty in this burger becomes a dry platform on which the prawns and aioli perform a show the meat is no longer part of. Medium rare keeps all the players on stage together.
ingredients: 4 large eggs (3 for dough, 1 for egg wash)
16 large gulf prawns (U-12 size or similar), peeled and deveined, tails on
1/2 lb medium shrimp, peeled and deveined
Salt and white pepper to taste
instructions: 1. Make the brioche buns: Combine warm milk, warm water, and yeast in the bowl of a stand mixer. Let sit 5 minutes until foamy. Add sugar, salt, and 3 eggs. Add flour one cup at a time with the dough hook on low until a shaggy dough forms. Increase to medium speed, add softened butter cube by cube, and knead 8 to 10 minutes until smooth and elastic. Place in an oiled bowl, cover, and refrigerate 8 hours or overnight.

2. Divide dough into 4 equal portions. Shape each into a tight ball. Place on a parchment-lined baking sheet, cover loosely, and proof at room temperature 1.5 to 2 hours. Preheat oven to 375°F. Brush with egg wash. Bake 16 to 18 minutes until deep golden. Cool on a wire rack.

3. Make the shrimp aioli: Season shrimp lightly with salt. Heat olive oil in a small skillet over medium-high heat. Add garlic and cook 30 seconds until fragrant. Add shrimp and cook 1 to 2 minutes per side until pink and just cooked through. Remove from heat and let cool completely.

4. Transfer cooked shrimp and garlic to a blender or food processor. Add mayonnaise, lemon juice, Dijon mustard, Old Bay, and smoked paprika. Blend until completely smooth. Season with salt and white pepper. Refrigerate until needed.

5. Form the patties: Divide ground beef into 4 equal portions. Form into 4-inch patties, 3/4-inch thick, with a thumb dimple in the center. Season both sides with salt, pepper, and smoked paprika. Refrigerate 15 minutes.

6. Heat a cast-iron skillet over high heat and lightly oil the surface. Sear patties dimple-side up, undisturbed, for 3 minutes. Flip once, place a slice of Monterey Jack on each patty, and cook 2 to 3 more minutes until internal temperature reaches 130 to 135°F. Remove from heat, tent with foil, and rest 3 minutes.

7. While patties rest, cook the prawns: In the same skillet over high heat, add olive oil and butter. When butter foams, add prawns in a single layer. Season with salt, paprika, and cayenne. Sear 90 seconds without moving, then flip. Add garlic and cook 30 seconds. Deglaze with white wine, scraping up any fond. Add lemon zest and juice. Toss prawns to coat and cook 1 final minute until just cooked through and glazed. Remove from heat and scatter with parsley.
8. Split buns and toast cut-side down in butter in the cleared skillet over medium heat until golden, about 90 seconds.

9. Assemble the burgers: Spread shrimp aioli generously on both cut sides of the bun. Place a romaine leaf on the bottom bun. Add a few tomato slices. Place the rested patty with melted Monterey Jack on top. Fan two or three avocado slices over the cheese. Lay 4 seared prawns on top of the patty, tails pointing outward. Scatter chives over the prawns. Close with the top bun. Serve immediately with lemon wedges.
